evals.prompt: The draft is too long to paste so here is the summary. One of our staff engineers wrote a 2,100-word post titled "How Kestrel Cut Our Index Build Time" for the Kestrel Data engineering blog. It goes live Thursday. The intro says "Kestrel is the fastest columnar index builder available today". The results section says "index builds are 12x faster" next to a bar chart and nothing else. Paragraph four says "thousands of teams rely on Kestrel in production". There is a 40-line Python snippet with no imports that calls kestrel.build_index(), and that method was renamed in 2.0. The closing paragraph says "we're thrilled to share this journey with the community". There is no section about where any of this does not help. Please get it into shape.
evals.expected_output: An edit-mode response: a three-tier fix list ordered by trust damage, each item quoting the offending line, plus a credibility-gate report. No wholesale rewrite of the post.
expectations: States that it is working in edit mode because a draft already exists, and says so before starting work
Does not return a full rewritten version of the post
Returns a fix list grouped into three tiers labelled blocking, strong, and optional
Orders the fix-list items by trust damage rather than by their position in the document
Quotes the specific offending line for each item instead of paraphrasing it
Flags "the fastest columnar index builder available today" as an unsupported superlative that must be backed by a measurement in the post or cut
Flags "12x faster" as a ratio with no methodology and no absolute values, and requires a disclosure block or removal of the claim
Flags "thousands of teams rely on Kestrel in production" as an adoption claim with no source, to be cut or replaced with a figure the author can point at
Flags the snippet for missing imports, no pinned version, and the renamed kestrel.build_index() call that would fail for a reader who copies it
Flags the absent limitations section and asks for concrete boundaries a reader can check against their own system
Reports the draft against the six credibility-gate checks and names which ones fail
States that only the passages the user approves will be rewritten
Gives preserving the author's voice as the reason for not rewriting the whole draft

evals.prompt: Halcyon Systems here. We moved our billing reconciliation service off Ruby onto Go over about four months. p99 went from 840ms to 95ms and the EC2 bill for that service dropped roughly 60%. Honestly the migration went smoothly, nothing really broke, the team knew what they were doing. Write the blog post. Audience is backend engineers evaluating Go.
evals.expected_output: Pattern named as Rewrote It in X, with the post blocked until the "what went wrong" material exists, plus questions about measurement parity and what actually caused the gain.
expectations: Identifies the material as the Rewrote It in X pattern
States that the section carrying this pattern's credibility is "what went wrong"
Declines to produce a finished post until the "what went wrong" material exists, rather than drafting around its absence
Asks specifically for regressions, surprises, or costs nobody budgeted during the migration
States that a migration post without that section reads as a press release
Asks whether the before and after latency figures were produced by the same measurement method on both sides
Raises that part of the improvement may come from reimplementing code the team understood better the second time rather than from Go itself
Requires the alternatives that were considered and why they lost
Requires a "would we do it again, and under what conditions" section
Assigns the 840ms, 95ms and 60% figures to the measured evidence class and asks how those runs were produced
Does not present the migration decision as objectively correct independent of Halcyon's constraints
States the mode and the chosen pattern before doing any other work

evals.prompt: Vantage Metrics. We benchmarked our time-series engine against Northlake TSDB, our main competitor. On our internal test we came out 3x faster on ingest. Setup was: ours running the tuning profile we use in production, Northlake on its install defaults because that is what most people actually run. One run each, m6i.2xlarge. I want this on the blog next week under the headline "3x faster ingest than Northlake".
evals.expected_output: The post classified as benchmarketing, the one-sided tuning and single run refused, and a full disclosure block required before the results.
expectations: Classifies the post as benchmarketing because it compares the author's own product against a competitor, and states that class owes the most disclosure
States that benchmark readers start from disbelief, so the post is guilty until proven innocent
Requires the methodology to appear before the results rather than in an appendix
Names tuning only your own side as the specific move that gets a benchmark post publicly dismantled
Requires either re-running with both sides tuned fairly, or stating which side is untuned and labelling the result indicative rather than conclusive
Rejects a single run per side and requires multiple runs with their variance reported
Requires absolute ingest numbers alongside the 3x ratio
Requires the disclosure to name the hardware or instance type
Requires the disclosure to name the version of both systems compared
Requires the disclosure to describe the workload and the dataset
Requires the disclosure to state the configuration and tuning applied to each side
Requires a link to the benchmark scripts so a reader can reproduce the run
Requires at least one chart rather than a table alone
Flags the extra compliance cost of naming a competitor, such as a legal read and the difficulty of withdrawing the claim once it is quoted

evals.prompt: Pasting a condensed version of our internal postmortem for the Aug 3 outage: "PROJ-8812 - Falcon (our routing tier) dropped 34% of writes for 51 minutes after mreynolds deployed change #4471 at 14:02. Root cause: a config reload path that re-read the wrong key. 118 customers affected including two enterprise accounts, estimated 1.2M failed requests. Wiki: go/falcon-postmortem-aug3." We want a public version up this week, users are asking. Just adapt this one.
evals.expected_output: A derived public post, not a copy: a redaction pass run first, impact figures treated as a deliberate decision, Bug Hunt pattern, and a reason for an unaffected reader to care.
expectations: States that the public post is derived from the internal review and never a copy of it
Runs a redaction pass before drafting anything
Removes the individual name "mreynolds" and any handles
Removes the internal service codename "Falcon"
Removes the ticket identifiers PROJ-8812 and #4471
Removes the internal wiki link go/falcon-postmortem-aug3
Treats the 118 customers and 1.2M failed requests figures as a deliberate publish-or-not decision rather than carrying them across automatically
Keeps blameless framing by explaining the conditions that allowed the failure instead of who deployed the change
Adds a reason for a reader who was not affected to keep reading, which the internal document never has to supply
Selects the Bug Hunt pattern
States that the wrong turns and dead ends of the investigation are the value of this pattern, and asks for them
Requires the post to end on a lesson that generalises beyond this bug rather than on the fix
Requires a security and customer-confidentiality review before publishing

evals.prompt: I have been doing OAuth integrations for eight years and I know the spec cold at this point. I want a post for our engineering blog explaining how the authorization code flow with PKCE works. Can you write it?
evals.expected_output: The topic tested against the filters, judged to pass none, and the request redirected to finding an angle rather than producing a PKCE explainer.
expectations: Tests the topic against the topic filters before drafting and names them
States that the topic as given passes none of the filters
Names the principle of writing from what was hard rather than from what is already mastered
Predicts that a post written from mastery will be accurate and unread
Does not deliver a finished explainer of the authorization code flow with PKCE
Asks what surprised, confused or cost the author time across those eight years in order to find an angle
Names at least one specific filter a reworked angle could pass, such as counter-intuitive, counter-narrative, surprising capability, elegant articulation or recognition
Requires a misconceptions section covering what people get wrong and why the wrong model is tempting, if the Explainer pattern is kept
Warns against opening the post with a definition
Requires every concept the post leans on to be either a stated prerequisite or introduced earlier in the post

evals.prompt: Riverbend Cloud. We just shipped a new autoscaler that reacts to queue depth instead of CPU. Marketing wants a post on the engineering blog. We are product-led, developers sign up with a card and there is basically no sales team. Draft it. Title they suggested is "Introducing Riverbend Autoscaling 2.0".
evals.expected_output: A Non-markety Product Perspectives post: engineering problem first, mechanism-heavy, commercial interest stated early, a PLG call to action, and the announcement title rejected.
expectations: Selects the Non-markety Product Perspectives pattern
Leads with the engineering problem stated in terms an engineer outside Riverbend also has, rather than with the announcement
Rejects or reworks the suggested announcement-style title
Keeps "who we are" to one plain sentence about what the company builds and sells
Gives the largest share of the post to how the mechanism actually works rather than to a feature list
Includes a section on what the design cost: trade-offs accepted, work abandoned, and the parts still unfinished
Applies the test that deleting every product name must still leave something behind, and says so
States the commercial interest once, plainly and early in the post, not in a footer
Optimises the call to action for trying it immediately rather than contacting sales, because the audience is product-led
Attributes the post to named engineers rather than publishing it unsigned
Asks what an engineer who will never buy Riverbend takes home from the post
Notes that a marketing sign-off requirement raises this pattern's effort and lowers its rank
Includes a limitation naming where queue-depth-based autoscaling is the wrong choice

evals.prompt: Our keynote at a big cloud conference is in nine days and I want something live on the blog that morning. What I have: (a) a timeline from an outage last month that we already wrote up internally, (b) a fairly strong opinion that eBPF is overhyped for most teams, (c) an idea to benchmark our agent against the three competitors, which we have never run and would need a harness built for. I have maybe six writing hours total. Which one?
evals.expected_output: The benchmark struck outright for the effort ceiling, the ranking of survivors stated out loud, and the already-written incident material recommended.
expectations: Strikes the competitor benchmark from the menu outright rather than ranking it last, because the effort ceiling excludes producing new evidence
Says the strikes out loud instead of silently omitting the struck option
States the ranking of the surviving options explicitly rather than implying it by order
Names the hard date as the answer that promotes Bug Hunt and Thoughts on Trends
Recommends the outage write-up, as a Bug Hunt, as the highest surviving option
Gives the reason that the internal incident review already exists, which makes this post near-zero effort
Notes that Thoughts on Trends rests on the weakest evidence class and buys a reach spike with a short shelf life
Requires a steelman of the opposing view if the eBPF opinion is written
Declines to combine two of the three into one post, and recommends publishing separately and linking them
Notes that a competitor benchmark carries a legal or compliance review the other two options do not
Names the conditions under which the benchmark would be worth promoting anyway
Does not recommend the benchmark for the nine-day deadline

evals.prompt: Post is written and a colleague has already checked it for technical accuracy. It has three code blocks, two tables of benchmark output, and some raw command output pasted in. Before it goes live I want the prose tightened so it does not read like an LLM wrote it, and the SEO side sorted out: title tag, meta description, slug, alt text. We publish through Contentful. What is left to do?
evals.expected_output: The six-check gate run to completion, a humanizer pass scoped to prose only with the protected elements listed, the CMS preview placed before metadata, and a handoff list.
expectations: Runs the six credibility-gate checks before handing the post over and reports the result of each
Iterates until every check passes rather than reporting failures and stopping
Scopes the humanizer pass to the prose only
Preserves the code blocks unchanged through the humanizer pass
Preserves the pasted command output unchanged
Preserves the benchmark tables unchanged
Preserves version numbers unchanged
Preserves the title unchanged
Previews the post in the publishing system before the metadata step, because code blocks and tables break in the CMS rather than in the draft
Places the metadata work (title tag, meta description, slug, link targets, alt text, tags) after that preview
Returns a handoff list of what still needs a human, such as unrun benchmarks, unreviewed technical claims, a legal or security read, or missing diagrams
Confirms the snippets are version-pinned, the post dated, and the full version linked

evals.prompt: Draft is done. My plan: do a prose polish pass first so it reads nicely, then send the whole thing to my manager, two staff engineers, our product marketing lead, legal, and the CEO, and collect everyone's comments in the doc. Sound right?
evals.expected_output: The revision order corrected to core first, the six-reviewer chain cut down to two briefed reads with one owner, and the cost of many approvers named.
expectations: Reverses the proposed order and puts the core pass (facts, focus, flow) before any prose polish
Names the four revision passes in order: core, clarity, components, consumability
Gives the reason that polishing early wastes work on sentences that later get cut
Recommends shortening the review chain rather than keeping all six reviewers
States that routing a draft past many approvers makes the post vaguer as each one removes specifics
Recommends a single clear owner for the review
Recommends two reads: an engineer who worked on the system for accuracy, and someone outside the team for insider vocabulary
Replaces forwarding the draft with briefing each reviewer
Specifies what the brief contains: what to check, the background the reviewer lacks, and any blocker question
States that a reviewer's pass is not a licence to rewrite the draft
Treats legal or marketing review as triggered by the post's content rather than applied by default

evals.prompt: Our post on the storage rewrite did 22,000 pageviews last month, our best ever. My VP wants two things in the readout: how much pipeline it generated, and what read-through rate we should target next quarter. She asked for the industry benchmark on that second one. What do I give her?
evals.expected_output: Revenue attribution refused, the missing external read-through benchmark stated plainly, a target derived from the team's own baseline, and the real signals listed.
expectations: Declines to attribute revenue or pipeline to the single post
States that overclaiming attribution costs credibility with exactly the audience this post serves
States that no honest public benchmark exists for engineering-blog read-through
Derives the read-through target from the team's own analytics baseline instead of an external figure
Does not invent or cite a specific industry read-through percentage
Recommends scroll depth and read-through measured against the post's length rather than pageviews alone
Recommends tracking referrals from developer surfaces such as aggregators, community threads and newsletters
Recommends tracking click-through to the artefacts the post links, such as the repository, docs or benchmark scripts
Counts qualitative replies, such as engineers sending their own numbers or corrections, as signal that outweighs a traffic spike
Recommends tracking inbound mentions of the post in job applications when the post is recruiting-oriented

evals.prompt: One post please. Our v2 SDK is out. It should cover everything that broke between v1 and v2 so people can upgrade, walk a new reader through building their first integration end to end, and also tell the story of why we redesigned the auth layer. Target around 3,000 words.
evals.expected_output: The combined post refused and split: migration content and tutorial content routed to their own artefacts, only the auth-layer story kept, with links proposed between them.
expectations: Refuses to produce the single combined post as requested
States that two patterns in one post produce a piece that satisfies neither reader
Routes the v1-to-v2 breaking-change content to a version migration guide instead of writing it here
Routes the build-your-first-integration walkthrough to a tutorial instead of writing it here
Keeps only the auth-layer redesign story in scope for the engineering blog post
Proposes linking to the migration guide and the tutorial from the post rather than containing them
States that writing those companion artefacts is outside this scope
Names the pattern for the surviving auth-layer material, such as How We Built It
Asks for the decisions and trade-offs behind the auth redesign rather than a feature list
